title: India Will Miss Its Budget Target for the First Time Since the Pandemic. The Iran War Just Blew a Hole in the Deficit.
excerpt: Authorities are willing to let the fiscal gap widen to 4.8 per cent of GDP as energy subsidies spiral, petrol prices climb, and the rupee slides to its worst year in a decade.
body:
India is preparing to miss its fiscal deficit target for the first time since the pandemic, Bloomberg News reported on Friday, as the Iran war's oil shock forces the government to spend far more on energy subsidies than anyone in New Delhi planned for.

Authorities are willing to let the budget gap widen to 4.8 per cent of GDP for the current fiscal year ending March 2027, half a percentage point above the 4.3 per cent target that Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman set in the February budget — days before the conflict with Iran broke out and rewired global energy markets.

The Finance Ministry has quietly told the major credit rating agencies that the slippage is entirely a product of external pressure, not a change in fiscal philosophy. The message to Moody's, S&P and Fitch: this is the oil talking, not a loosening of the purse strings.

**The numbers behind the blowout are stark.** India imports more than 85 per cent of its crude, and roughly half of pre-war supply came through the Strait of Hormuz, which has been effectively shut since Tehran curtailed shipping in retaliation for U.S. strikes. State-owned fuel retailers have already raised petrol and diesel prices four times in May alone — an 8 per cent jump — and the government has cut cooking gas subsidies for households. The fertiliser subsidy bill is projected to surge 20 per cent this fiscal year.

Chief Economic Adviser V. Anantha Nageswaran told NDTV on Friday that the Reserve Bank of India's 6.6 per cent GDP growth projection, with a downside risk of 20 to 30 basis points, remains "realistic." That is a sharp comedown from the 7.0 to 7.4 per cent range Nageswaran himself projected in February, before the Middle East went up in flames.

The rupee has already fallen more than 5 per cent since the war began, making it the worst-performing Asian currency of 2026. Foreign investors have pulled a record $30 billion out of Indian equities this year, pivoting to semiconductor-heavy markets in South Korea and Taiwan. India's current account deficit is forecast to blow out to 2.5 per cent of GDP, up from 0.9 per cent last year.

**For NRIs, the fiscal slippage carries direct consequences.** A wider deficit means higher government borrowing, which could crowd out private credit and keep interest rates elevated longer than expected. The RBI is already walking a tightrope — it cut rates earlier this year to support growth, but renewed inflation pressure from fuel prices (consumer inflation hit a new-series high of 3.93 per cent in May) is narrowing its room to manoeuvre.

The silver lining, if there is one: Nageswaran suggested that fuel retailers may not need to pass on much more of the oil price hike to consumers, provided global prices settle lower over the full year as financial markets expect. And authorities are keeping their options open — a reassessment of the fiscal outlook is planned for later this year, once there is more clarity on non-tax revenues and subsidy needs. Spending cuts across ministries are also on the table.

But the fiscal guardrails that India spent years rebuilding after the pandemic are now being tested by a conflict it played no part in starting. The last time India missed its deficit target was in 2020-21, when COVID-19 forced emergency spending of a different kind. This time, the emergency is arriving through oil tankers, not hospital wards.

*Sources: Bloomberg News, Reuters, NDTV, OilPrice.com, The Hindu Business Line*
